Quite for Cookies

See it before you delete it.

See every cookie a site has stored, delete only what you pick, and watch it check that the deletion actually worked. Or have it clear each site as you close its last tab.

Free MIT ChromeEdgeBraveArc

Add to Chrome, it's free View the source ›

5 permissions · No site access until you ask · No tracking · MIT licensed

Most cookie cleaners delete first and tell you nothing. Quite for Cookies shows you the list before anything is removed. Every cookie the site has stored, grouped by the domain that set it, with sizes. The ones that keep you signed in are marked as such, and left alone unless you say otherwise. Local storage, databases, caches and service workers are listed alongside them.

Removal is cookie by cookie rather than a blunt sweep of the whole site, so unticking a domain genuinely spares it. Afterwards the extension counts again and reports the result: how many went, how many could not be removed, and how many the page has already set again because it is still open. Those numbers come from re-reading the browser, never from assuming the delete worked.

It can also do the job without being asked. Turn on “clear a site when I close its last tab” and the sweep runs in the background as you browse, sparing sign-ins and anything on your spared list. Chrome’s own session-only setting cannot do this. It waits until you close the whole browser. Every sweep is recorded and shown in the popup, so a run that cleared nothing can never be mistaken for one that worked.

What it does

8 things, and no more.

The list comes first

Every cookie the site has stored, grouped by the domain that set it, with sizes. Nothing is removed until you have seen it and pressed the button.

Sign-in cookies are marked

The ones holding your session are flagged and spared by default, so cleaning a site does not quietly log you out of it.

Cookie by cookie, not all or nothing

Untick a domain and it is genuinely left alone. No blunt “clear everything for this site” that takes your other subdomains with it.

It checks afterwards

After deleting it counts again and reports what actually went, what could not be removed, and what the page has already set again because it is still open.

Clear a site as you close it

Switch it on and closing a site’s last tab clears it, in the background, without you doing anything. Sign-ins and anything on your spared list are left alone, and a second tab still open on the same site stops the sweep.

Every sweep is recorded

The background job runs where nobody is watching, so it writes down what it did. A sweep that removed nothing says so, rather than looking the same as one that worked.

Or sweep the whole browser

A second tab cleans every site at once. The default removes advertising and analytics cookies only, matched against known tracking domains. It cannot sign you out, because nothing you can log in to is on that list.

No access until you ask

It installs with no permission to see any site. Access is requested one domain at a time, at the moment you press the button, and is reversible from the popup.

Installing it

One click from the Chrome Web Store. The unpacked route below still works if you would rather run the source.

Add to Chrome

  1. 1

    Download the latest release and unzip it. You need the folder. Keep it somewhere permanent, because moving or deleting it stops the extension working.

  2. 2

    Open chrome://extensions in your browser.

  3. 3

    Turn on Developer mode, top right.

  4. 4

    Click Load unpacked and select the folder you unzipped.

  5. 5

    Reload any site you were looking at tab you already had open.

Chrome shows a "Developer mode extensions" warning each time it starts. That is normal for anything installed outside the Web Store, and it can be dismissed.

Latest news

Releases and breakages for Quite for Cookies.

30 August 2026 Fixed Quite for Cookies

Quite for Cookies 0.22.7: the “trackers only” sweep could sign you out

The default sweep is called Trackers only, and until this version the popup told you it could not sign you out of anything, because nothing on its list of tracking domains was a site you could log in to.

That was not true. The list included analytics and marketing products, among them HubSpot, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Segment, Optimizely and New Relic, whose own customers sign in on those same addresses. The sweep matched the address rather than the cookie, so on those sites it removed everything, sign-in cookies included. If you use any of those tools for work, a sweep may have signed you out of them.

The safety promise was written in a comment rather than enforced in the code. It is now enforced. Anything that looks like a sign-in is spared in both sweeps, and the checkbox that controls it works in both. It used to be greyed out in the default sweep, so it could not even be switched on.

Three other ways data could go that should not have are fixed in the same release. Closing a tab in an Incognito window could clear the ordinary profile's cookies and stored data for that site. Unticking a row did not always protect it, when two cookies shared an address. And a site with no cookies could never be added to the spared list, while the automatic clear would still wipe its stored data.

Nothing about this was reported by a user. It came out of an audit we ran on our own published code before adding a fourth extension.

Every setting

Click the extension icon. Changes apply immediately.

OptionDefaultWhat it does
This site Tab What the site you are on has stored, grouped by who set it.
Every site Tab One sweep across the whole browser.
Trackers only On Advertising and analytics cookies. Cannot sign you out.
Everything Off All cookies and site data. Says plainly that it will sign you out.
Keep sign-in cookies On Spares the cookies holding your session.
Include other companies’ cookies Off Cookies set by domains the page loaded, rather than the site itself.
Clear a site when I close its last tab Off Runs on its own, in the background. Sites on your spared list are never touched. Needs access to every site.
Keep sign-in cookies when it does On Leaves anything that looks like a login, so closing a tab tidies the tracking without logging you out.
Also clear stored site data Off Without it, trackers keeping a copy of your ID in local storage put the same cookie straight back.

What it asks for

Five permissions, and no access to any site until you ask for it. Here is why each is there.

activeTab
To read the address of the tab you are on when you click the icon, so everything can be scoped to that one site. Nothing is read from the page until you press a button.
cookies
To list and delete cookies. This is what the extension is for.
browsingData
To clear local storage, databases, caches and service workers, restricted to the site you are looking at.
scripting
To run a short read-only snippet in the page that counts the cookies the page itself can see. This is what makes the preview accurate rather than approximate.
storage
To remember which domains you have chosen to spare on each site, and the totals shown in the popup. Nothing leaves your browser.
None at install
Unlike the other two, this one starts with no access to any site at all. When you press “Show what this site stored”, it asks for the one domain you are on, and nothing else. Clearing sites automatically as you close them does need browser-wide access, because it has to see which site a closing tab belonged to. That one is asked for separately, only if you switch it on, and taken back from the same line of text in the popup.

Chrome shows you this list at install time. We would rather you saw it first. The source is public, so you can check that it is the whole list.

Questions

Will it sign me out?

Not unless you ask it to. Cookies that hold your session are marked and spared by default, the whole-browser sweep defaults to advertising and analytics cookies only, and the automatic clear keeps sign-ins too. The options that do sign you out say so where you turn them on.

What does “clear a site when I close its last tab” actually do?

When the last tab for a site closes, it clears that site’s cookies in the background. If you still have the site open in another tab, nothing happens. Sites on your spared list are never touched, and sign-in cookies are kept unless you turn that off. Chrome’s own session-only setting cannot do this. It waits until you close the entire browser.

Why does it need access to a site?

Chrome’s activeTab permission does not cover the cookies API, so reading a site’s cookies genuinely requires host access. Asking for one registrable domain at the moment you press the button is the narrowest form of that. It is granted per site, and revoked from the same line of text in the popup. The automatic clear is the exception: it has to watch tabs closing, so it needs browser-wide access before it will run.

How is this different from clearing cookies in Chrome?

Chrome clears without showing you what was there, and works on the whole site. This lists everything first, grouped by the domain that set it, lets you spare individual domains, and counts again afterwards to check the removal actually worked.

Some cookies came back straight away.

If the page is still open it can set them again the moment they go. The report says so explicitly rather than showing a tick. That is the point of counting a second time. Trackers that keep a copy of your ID in local storage do the same thing, which is what the “also clear stored site data” option is for.
